title: Delaware (Lenape) in the 1780 Kentucky raids
summary: Lenape bands hunted and wintered south of the Ohio, and Delaware warriors joined Capt. Henry Bird’s British-Native column that invaded Kentucky in 1780.
bodyMarkdown:
The [Lenape](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lenape), called the Delaware by the English, began far from Kentucky. Their homeland ran along the Delaware River and the coast of what is now New Jersey, eastern Pennsylvania, and southern New York. Colonial land deals, including the 1737 [Walking Purchase](https://grokipedia.com/page/Walking_Purchase), pushed them west. By the 1750s many Lenape lived in the Ohio country.

From those towns north of the Ohio, Lenape bands hunted and wintered south of the river, alongside Shawnee, Mingo, and others. The story of [Delaware winter camps on Kentucky ground](/stories/delaware-winter-camps-on-kentucky-ground/) tells that side of it.

During the Revolution the Lenape tried at first to stay neutral. In 1778 the Treaty of Fort Pitt made some of them allies of the United States, the first Indian treaty the new nation signed. It did not hold. The pro-American leader White Eyes died that fall, under suspicious circumstances, and American militia attacks on Lenape towns turned many against the Americans.

In the summer of 1780, a British officer, [Henry Bird](/people/#henry-bird), led a column of British soldiers, Canadian militia, and several hundred Native warriors out of Detroit. They came up the Licking with small cannon, something no Kentucky fort could stand against. Delaware warriors were among the nations in that force. In late June, Ruddle's Station surrendered, and Martin's Station fell the next day. Hundreds of settlers were marched north as captives. Some were adopted into Native families. Others were held near Detroit until later exchanges, and a few did not come home until after the [Treaty of Greenville](/stories/treaty-of-greenville-1795-the-line-to-the-kentucky-river/) in 1795.

Accounts differ on Bird's rank. Many histories call him Captain Henry Bird, while the [ExploreKYHistory marker text](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/591) calls him "Colonel Henry Byrd."

[George Rogers Clark](/people/#george-rogers-clark) answered that August with a strike on the Shawnee towns at Piqua. The war on both sides of the Ohio went on for another fourteen years.

## Kentucky today

State historical markers in Bourbon and Harrison counties recall the 1780 raid on Ruddle's and Martin's stations. The Lenape are not gone. Two federally recognized nations carry the name: the [Delaware Nation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Delaware_Nation) at Anadarko, Oklahoma, and the Delaware Tribe of Indians at Bartlesville, Oklahoma.
Source: [Grokipedia: Lenape](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lenape)
